question: Why can a pipeline architecture achieve viable real-time conversation performance despite chaining three separate models?
options: The pipeline skips stages when latency is too high
The models are very small and fast
Each stage streams into the next — STT sends partial transcripts, LLM streams tokens, TTS synthesizes from the first sentence — so stages run concurrently
WebRTC compresses the data between stages
explanation: The pipeline works because each stage streams into the next. STT does not wait for the user to finish before sending partial transcripts. The LLM does not wait for the full transcript. TTS does not wait for the full response. This pipelining makes the architecture viable despite having three separate models.

question: A healthcare company needs complete text transcripts of every patient conversation for regulatory compliance. Which architecture should they prefer?
options: Hybrid — switch to pipeline only for compliance-sensitive turns
Pipeline — it naturally produces text transcripts at the STT and LLM stages
Either architecture works equally well for this requirement
explanation: The pipeline architecture naturally produces text transcripts at the STT stage (user speech) and LLM stage (agent response). Realtime models process audio end-to-end and can produce transcripts, but it is not their primary output. For regulated industries requiring complete transcript logging, the pipeline provides this naturally.

question: What is the primary reason realtime models have lower latency than pipeline architectures?
options: They skip the LLM reasoning step entirely
They collapse three model round-trips into a single model inference, eliminating cascading delays
explanation: A pipeline accumulates latency across three separate model calls (STT, LLM, TTS), each with its own network round-trip and processing time. A realtime model handles everything in a single inference pass with one network round-trip, eliminating the cascading delays that add up to 500-1200ms in a pipeline.
